s01.slug: FRIDAY · 3:12 AM · DELGADO HALL, THE FRONT LAWN
body: Fifty-eight minutes after *Goodnight, Jack*, Delgado Hall goes off. It’s the goose again, the same flat, outraged horn as the first time, strobes stuttering down every hallway, three hundred and ten freshmen coming down the stairwells in whatever they sleep in. Jack wasn’t asleep, which saves him a step. He goes down the east stairs in yesterday’s flannel and yesterday’s jeans, still smelling faintly of the Hobart, the RAZR shut in his pocket on a text he hasn’t deleted and isn’t going to.

Out on the lawn the fog has come in off the Lagoon to the knee, and it beads on everything wool: sweaters, blankets, one girl’s entire Snuggie. The tide is out, and the Lagoon smells like the back room of a bait shop. The eucalyptus drips. Over in the Anacapa lot the sodium lamps have gone orange in the fog, and everybody standing under them looks jaundiced and personally wronged.

On the lobby steps Priya stands in her Fremont High hoodie with the air horn in one hand and, held over her head in the other like a picket sign for a strike with one member, a single laminate: THE LAWN IS NOT A SOCIAL EVENT. She says nothing. She has said it all in writing.

The roll call is Kevin’s. Clipboard, navy quarter-zip zipped to the sternum over plaid pajama pants, a flag-football voice that carries without yelling. “Pruitt?” Nothing. Kevin looks east without being told. At the far end of the building, out the wrong fire door, Doug Pruitt stands barefoot on the wet concrete with his pillow under his arm. “Pruitt’s here.” Kevin gets to Jack and takes him in from the sneakers up. “Costigan. Present, and fully dressed, at three in the morning.” The pen makes its check. “I don’t ask questions, bro. I just take attendance.”

Margot is off by herself at the edge of the lamplight in a black peacoat over black, visibly not cold, the Moleskine open. She doesn’t look up when he stops beside her. She writes, and tilts the page so he can read it by strobe: ALARM 2. “Eighteen days,” she says. “That’s not a schedule. That’s a person.” She clicks the pen shut and goes back to the crowd, working through it methodically, face by face, left to right.
Theo comes out among the last, barefoot in the navy silk robe, with the gray camera bag on one shoulder and the black one on the other and nothing in his hands. “No espresso machine?” “It’s insured.”
“FIREMAN.”

Laney comes across the lawn with her arms already up. She’s been home two hours from her first night as a Pi Lam, and it shows in the best way: Thursday’s pink PI LAM RODEO tee under the gray Cardinal Mooney hoodie that stopped being Jack’s at the first alarm, the hoodie to her knees, and on top of everything the pink straw cowboy hat, tipped back. “They were *lucky*, fireman,” she says, and gets him around the neck. “You *said*.” She lets go to turn a slow circle on the wet grass, one hand on the hat. “I was adored, sugar. *Professionally*.” Then she takes the hat off, sets it on Jack’s head, squares it with both thumbs and pats the crown. “Hold this, fireman.” And she’s off into the fog, yelling somebody’s name.

The hat is still on his head when Lena finds him. The black WHO DAT shirt, the oatmeal cardigan buttoned one hole off, Keds with the laces dragging, her hair up in a knot she did in the dark. She looks at the hat. Then she looks at him under it. “Goodnight,” she says, “was premature.”

She tucks her hands up into the cardigan sleeves. “Becca Lindell wrote on your wall.” They’ve been Facebook friends since the first week of classes, and Becca’s post has been up since Tuesday at 12:41 a.m., two exclamation points and a smiley face, for anybody who cared to look. Somebody cared to look. “It’s a beach cleanup, Jack. It is not a date. Bring gloves.”

journal.title: Fire alarms, 3 a.m.
journal.text: Alarm 1, Monday the 31st, 3:07: everybody on the lawn in what they sleep in; Theo saved the espresso machine; Margot wrote ‘ALARM 1’ like it was a case number. Alarm 2, Friday the 18th, 3:12: eighteen days. Margot says that’s not a schedule, it’s a person. She’s keeping a log.

choices.text: “Gloves are a big step for me.”
response: “Then you’re not ready, Costigan.” She doesn’t look at him to say it. She looks enormously pleased with herself instead, chin tucked down into the cardigan collar.

At 3:36 the strobes quit and three hundred and ten people squeak back across the grass toward the doors. Laney goes in leaning her whole weight on Lena, a parade float being towed home by a much smaller car, and on the way past she lifts her hat off Jack’s head without looking at him and puts it back on her own.
“I’m Newman, Costigan. I’ll be picking up Las Olas’s sins with tongs.” She considers the fog. “They hand out those grabber sticks. I intend to get one before Joey Abruzzo does, or he’ll grab people.”

At 3:36 the strobes quit and the lawn squeaks back inside. Laney comes out of the fog and drapes herself over Lena from behind, every ounce, and Lena takes it without breaking stride. Going past, Laney lifts the hat off Jack’s head, no look, no thank-you, and puts it back where it belongs.

“I know. I’m the one who said so.” She looks out at the fog instead of at him, and whatever she means to say next is still on its way when the strobes quit at 3:36 and three hundred and ten people start squeaking back across the grass.

Laney arrives out of nowhere and hangs her whole weight off Lena’s shoulders, and Lena walks her toward the doors like that, a girl wearing a girl. On the way past, Laney lifts the hat off Jack’s head without a glance and puts it back on her own.

body.title: From: Adrian Hale · To: John Costigan · Thu, Sep 17, 2009, 11:58 PM · Subject: Friday
body.text: Mr. Costigan — Friday, 2:30, my office. Bring the O’Connor in your back pocket; I want to see what a man underlines in it. —A.H.

body: It went to him alone: no cc line, no seminar. For a man who has never once located the BCC field, that’s practically a sealed letter.

Hollis 314 is at the end of the third-floor hall, behind a door with a pebbled-glass pane and HALE in gold leaf that’s been flaking since the first Clinton administration. Inside, the window is the whole Pacific, blue to the top of the glass, the kelp beds dark under the swell. The carpet is a green nobody chose, with a wine stain by the desk in the exact shape of Italy, boot and all. There are shelves, but the books have left them. They stand in stacks on the floor, knee-high, waist-high, with streets between them and one avenue to the desk: a city with no planning board. On the hook behind the door hangs a leash, and there’s no dog.

Hale is in the linen jacket, the wine on the cuff gone the brown of an old map, his reading glasses pushed up into the silver hair. He doesn’t get up. He holds out one hand, palm up, and it takes Jack a second to understand it isn’t for shaking.

He goes through the O’Connor with a licked thumb for every page, as if it were the racing form, and Jack sits across the desk and watches the most famous atheist in California read his margins. Hale reads them out loud. “‘NO.’ ‘Coward.’ ‘Okay, *fine*.’” He looks up over the pages with open delight. “You write in the margins like a man shouting at a referee.” He turns a page. “So did I.”

Then he reaches behind him without looking, into a stack that ought to fall over and doesn’t, and comes out with a paperback: Bernard Williams, *Moral Luck*, Cambridge, 1981, the spine gone soft as an old shirt. He opens it on the desk between them. Pencil, all down the margins, in a hand thirty years younger than the one across the desk. *No.* Three pages on: *Bernard, really.* “Bring it back,” Hale says, “with your margins in it.”

Jack takes the Benedict holy card out of the O’Connor, where it has been keeping the Misfit’s place since Sunday, and slides it into the Williams. Hale watches the Pope go into Bernard Williams and keeps his face perfectly still. The Williams goes in Jack’s back pocket, where it fits as if it were built for one.

Hale sits back. The chair complains. He folds his hands on his stomach and considers Jack, pleasantly, as if he were weather. Then, gently, as if asking the time: “You said no. The lucky one doesn’t sleep.” The glasses stay up in his hair. “How would you know, at eighteen?”

journal.title: Prof. Adrian Hale
journal.text: Wrote *The Consolations of Disbelief*. Wrote me a postcard. Walked into Hollis 302 at 1:07 with wine on his cuff and asked us to prove we have souls. Saw my face at the Anchor before he could put it to the nine pages. Called me a spaniel. Some nights he drinks alone in the Anchor’s back booth after midnight and says Housman to the window. Tips like he’s apologizing. Wrote his doctorate on moral luck. Asked me if the lucky one sleeps. Lent me his own copy of Williams’s *Moral Luck*, his Oxford pencil arguing with Williams in the margins on a first-name basis. Wants it back with mine in it.

choices.key: You told Hale your brother is in prison.
response: He gives Hale the version he gives anybody who gets one. A fight. A guy got hurt bad. Five years. Danny pleaded.

For once nothing clever is waiting on Hale’s face. What arrives first is plain decency, and it’s a while before anything follows it in. People ask how long. Hale asks, “What do you send him?” “A book a month. Used. They make me erase the margins.”

Hale takes the glasses down out of his hair and holds them by one arm. “Erased,” he says. Then: “That is the most obscene thing I’ve heard this week, and I have read the Baucus draft.” Somewhere under the window a lawnmower starts up and quits. “Thank you for telling me, Mr. Costigan.” He says it plainly, and puts the glasses back up on his head, where he’ll lose them by five.

choices.text: “My dad’s been laid off since June. I know what a man looks like who doesn’t sleep.”
response: Hale looks at him across the stacks. “Do you,” he says, and leaves it a statement. He doesn’t push. The pen stays where it’s lying on the blotter. For a while he looks out at the water, and Jack looks at the leash on the hook, and the garage on Glenwood Avenue sits in the room with them, the radio on low, a man in a folding chair at two in the morning.
Then Hale asks what Jack made of Williams’s lorry driver, and they talk about that instead, and it’s the most tact Jack has ever seen out of him.

“Nobody reads ahead in my class, Mr. Costigan. They read *around*.” He lets Jack have it. He tips back in the complaining chair and enjoys it openly, and the enjoyment is the price: Jack gets out from under the question, and Hale gets to watch him do it, and they both know which of them got the better seat.

choices.text: “It’s a seminar, Professor. I argued the side.”
response: “No,” Hale says, “you didn’t.” And then, as if he hadn’t said it, he’s off on Gauguin: Williams’s Gauguin, who leaves a wife and five children for Tahiti, and if the paintings are bad he’s a shit, and if they’re good he’s still a shit but a justified one, and nothing he decided on the dock decides which. “Justified by the weather, Mr. Costigan. Isn’t that monstrous? I’ve loved it for thirty years.”
He talks for a full minute, beautifully, and never once looks at Jack, which is how Jack knows the question is still on the desk between them.

s02b.slug: FRIDAY · 3:58 PM · HOLLIS HALL, THE FRONT STEPS
body: At four minutes to four Hale gets up, which he hasn’t done in an hour and a half, and walks Jack to the door through the streets of books. He stops with one hand on the frame.

body.text: “Miss Broussard was here at two,” he says. “She didn’t want to talk about why.”
body.else: “Miss Broussard was here at two,” he says. “She also didn’t want to talk about why.”

body: “Her paper is the best thing a freshman has handed me in ten years. You’ll not tell her I said so. She’d be unbearable.” The door is already closing. “And she’d be right.”

Outside, the Hollis steps are warm through his jeans. Bougainvillea comes down over the arcade in a magenta landslide, and below it the Commons is full of four o’clock sun, a Frisbee, a kid asleep under the *Tide*. The RAZR has been buzzing against the Williams for twenty minutes. He opens it to the angle where the screen works.

body.text: 412. Made you something. Come look. Bring nothing. —T.V.
I NEED A PALLBEARER. MISSION ST. NOW. —M

body: A Portland number he never saved, because she has never once used it on him. The Nokia doesn’t do lowercase. Neither does Margot.

choices.text: Mission Street. Somebody has to carry the coffin.

body: Theo is cross-legged on his bed in a gray cashmere sweater with the MacBook Pro on his knees, the 5D’s card reader trailing off one side of it and the iPhone tethered to the other, and on the screen is a timeline in Final Cut, stripes of color stacked up like a layer cake. He doesn’t look up. “Sit. Not on the bed. The bed is the edit bay.”

It’s called WEEK ONE, in a title card Theo has spent longer on than any paper: the beach below the bluff that first Friday, firelight, Laney informing the Pacific *who dat*; Sully’s on Sunday, the brass bell, Laney on the table in sequins. The cuts land on the beat. A shot of Kevin catching a falling fry holds exactly as long as it’s funny and not one frame longer. Theo is good at this. Jack can tell how good by how hard he’s working to look bored. “It’s for a class,” Theo says. “What class?” “The class I’m taking in my room.”

Jack takes Theo’s grandfather’s cufflinks out of the top drawer, where they’ve been since Sunday, gold, plain, heavy for their size, and sets them on Theo’s desk. Theo glances over. “Keep them for the Eagles.” “They’re your grandfather’s.” “He’d have liked the Eagles less.” Jack leaves them on the desk anyway, side by side, where Theo can look at them or not.

body: He reads it standing up. Then he turns the RAZR around and holds it out, and Theo takes his hands off the keyboard. “A girl at school said something about Danny,” Jack says. “Gina said his name back.” Theo reads to the end. “Your sister,” he says, “is a killer.” Then the eyebrow. “The nun?” “Nonna’s word. Same girl as the veil girl.”

Theo looks delighted for about a second, two of his favorite storylines having turned out to be one storyline. Then the delight goes, and what replaces it is shorter. “Has she met him?” “Thursday. On the bench. She said hi.” Theo nods once. “Good.”

He drags the playhead without asking. “Forty seconds. I was going to wait till it was finished.” He drops it to quarter speed. Sully’s, halftime, from table height: the iPhone propped against the ketchup the whole time, apparently, while Jack thought Theo was just sitting there with his chin on his fist. Lena leaning across the booth with Laney’s gold pencil. Her hand along Jack’s jaw, her thumb at the corner of his mouth. The stroke of gold going on, slow as poured honey at this speed. And Jack, on a laptop screen in Room 412, holding absolutely still, the way you hold still when a bird has landed on you and you’d like it to stay.

Theo pauses it on a frame. “Look at your face, Costigan.” Jack looks. He’d rather not have. Theo keeps his eyes on the screen. “What are you doing?” It isn’t a bit. Nobody else in Jack’s life is going to ask him that. Theo asks.

journal.title: Gina
journal.text: My sister. Fifteen, a sophomore at Ursuline. Texts in lowercase like punctuation costs extra. A girl in religion class called her the class expert on visiting the imprisoned. Dad turned the radio back on. Nonna told the altar society I went to confession. Gina wants to know if the nun is real. Said Danny’s name back to the girl. The girl looked away first. Then laughed with Kelsey anyway. Gina wants the first part on the record.

choices.key: You told Theo you don’t know what you’re doing.
response: Theo nods slowly. “Okay,” he says. “That’s the right answer. It’s also the worst one.” He saves the cut, Command-S, the little wheel turning, and closes the file.

Then he’s himself again, stretching until his spine cracks. “Sloane Kittredge has invited me to a barn. Tomorrow night, Pi Lam, Laney’s first party as a sister. I’ll be wearing hay.” “I work till one.” “Then come at one. Barns don’t close.”

choices.text: “She’s taken, Theo. I’m not doing anything.”
response: “That’s what I mean,” Theo says, and closes the laptop with one finger. The screen goes, and the room is only the room again, late sun lying across the crucifix over Jack’s bed.

Theo lies back on the edit bay. “Sloane Kittredge has invited me to a barn. Tomorrow night, Pi Lam, Laney’s first party as a sister. I’ll be wearing hay.” “I work till one.” “Then come at one. Barns don’t close.”

Theo laughs, really laughs, head back against the wall. Then he scrubs back to the top, to the title card, and lets WEEK ONE run again from the beginning, Laney and the Pacific, the bell at Sully’s, every frame of it where he left it. “You’ll need representation,” he says, watching his own cut with frank love.
“Sloane Kittredge has invited me to a barn, by the way. Tomorrow night, Pi Lam, Laney’s first party as a sister. I’ll be wearing hay.” “I work till one.” “Then come at one. Barns don’t close.”

s03b.slug: FRIDAY · 4:05 PM · MISSION STREET, HARBOR SMOKE & CIGAR
body: Harbor Smoke & Cigar has never been within a mile of the harbor. It’s at the near end of Mission Street, where the road comes off Ocean Road past the campus gate, in a stucco strip between a laundromat and a tattoo parlor called Sacred Heart that Jack has decided not to have an opinion about. La Flaca gets him there in seven minutes, the coaster brake shrieking at the light.

Inside it’s cedar and cold and dim, the humidors along one wall glowing like aquariums, a bell over the door that goes on faintly ringing after it shuts. Margot is at the counter in black with the peacoat over her arm and a coin purse open on the glass. The clerk, sixties, cardigan, reading glasses on a chain, has been selling her cloves since August, and today he speaks to her in the voice of a funeral director. “Tuesday,” he says. “The twenty-second. After that it’s menthol or nothing. Congress.” He sets a carton on the glass and rests his palm flat on top of it. “That’s the last Djarum Black between here and San Luis Obispo.”

Margot pays to the cent: bills unfolded from the coin purse one at a time, then quarters, then two dimes, then a nickel she has to dig for. The clerk waits with his hands folded. She takes the carton, turns, and hands it to Jack. “At shoulder height,” she says. “You’re a pallbearer. Conduct yourself.”

Out on the sidewalk she gives him the arrangements. “The wake is Tuesday. The Delgado roof, at sundown. Bring the other Catholic.” She checks the sky, as if sundown might be early out of spite. “Rosh Hashanah starts tonight, incidentally. My father observes it as a seminar. There’s a reading list. There’s an apple.” In his pocket the RAZR buzzes against the Williams.

body: Margot reads it upside down off the RAZR while he’s still reading it right side up, and says nothing about it at all.

She’s going to the chastity talk at Newman tonight. “For the *Tide*,” she says. “There’s no faith page. There will be.” They start for the bus stop at the corner, bearing the carton between them like a very small casket, at a height she keeps correcting with one finger. Halfway there, without changing her tone in the slightest, she says, “Why wait?” He looks at her. She keeps her eyes on the street. “Actually. Not the pamphlet.”

journal.title: Gina
journal.text: My sister. Fifteen, a sophomore at Ursuline. Texts in lowercase like punctuation costs extra. A girl in religion class called her the class expert on visiting the imprisoned. Dad turned the radio back on. Nonna told the altar society I went to confession. Gina wants to know if the nun is real. Said Danny’s name back to the girl. The girl looked away first. Then laughed with Kelsey anyway. Gina wants the first part on the record.

choices.text: Give her the real case. No pamphlet.
response: So he gives her his own. That the body isn’t a rental. That he isn’t scared of wanting: the wanting is *good*, the wanting is the whole point, it’s about the best thing anybody ever made, and that’s exactly why you don’t hand it out on Mission Street like a flyer for somebody’s band. That he’d like it to mean what it says when he finally says it. He hears himself getting loud on a public sidewalk at four in the afternoon with a carton of clove cigarettes held at shoulder height, and keeps going anyway.

Margot hears him out the whole way to the bus stop. There she takes the carton back. “Lena said the same thing,” she says, “with more Latin.” So they’ve had this one out without him. He finds he’d have paid to watch.

choices.text: “Half the time I don’t know if I can.”
choices.key: You told Margot the truth: half the time you don’t know if you can wait.
response: Margot says nothing. They reach the stop. The bus comes in and kneels at the curb with a long hydraulic sigh, and opens, and waits, and nobody gets on, and the driver gives them a look and closes up and pulls away.

Margot watches it go. “That’s the first honest thing a Catholic’s said to me about it,” she says. She doesn’t write it down. She takes the carton back out of his hands, carefully, at shoulder height, and holds it against her coat while they wait for the next one.

choices.text: “Cloves are banned in four days. Some of us plan ahead.”
response: Margot nearly laughs. He watches it get as far as the corner of her mouth and get turned back at the border. “Coward,” she says, almost fondly.
At the bus stop she takes the carton back and holds it against her chest, squared and level, like a folded flag.

body: He never sleeps. He lies on top of the blanket from a little after four with the Williams on his chest, unopened, sand still in his shoes on the floor, and at 5:40 he gives up and goes down the hall for water.

The fourth-floor lounge is gray and empty, the Zenith dark on its cart. Priya’s laminate from last week is still taped to the whiteboard frame at its angle of struggle, and under it Margot’s capitals have gone up again since Friday night, while he was busy.

body: He drinks the water at the lounge window. Gray light is coming up behind the Grove, the eucalyptus black against it, the Lagoon flat as pewter. By six he’s back on his bed.

At ten past six the door opens and Theo comes in barefoot, with sand on his feet and the hems of his good jeans dark and wet to the shin, and hay still caught in the cashmere from the barn. He doesn’t turn the light on. He sits on the edge of his bed and starts picking straw off his sleeve one piece at a time.
“She woke up at four,” he says. Laney. “She asked for a waffle and her mother. Sloane produced a waffle.” He flicks a straw at the wastebasket and misses.

body.text: Jack reaches over to the desk and finds Theo’s grandfather’s cufflinks in the half dark by feel, and holds them out across the gap between the beds. Theo looks at them in his palm. “Keep them for the Eagles.” “They’re your grandfather’s.” “He’d have liked the Eagles less.” Jack sets them on Theo’s nightstand anyway.

body: Jack is looking at the jeans. Theo answers the look. “I run now,” he says, working at a knot of hay in his cuff. “Four miles. Barefoot. It’s very good for the lymphatic system.”

journal.title: Theo, before light
journal.text: Came in barefoot at 5:20, sand and wet jeans. ‘Couldn’t sleep.’ There was a girl in our room. Sunday the 20th, 6:10, wet to the shins and hay on his sweater: he says he runs now. Four miles. Barefoot.

journal.title: The whiteboard
journal.text: Margot’s, by annexation: USEFUL IDIOTS FOR CHRISTIAN NATIONALISM, COSTIGAN | BROUSSARD. The chastity talk made the board: both of us, voluntarily. Kenzie Rourke got her own line. Margot thinks she might not be an idiot. Category pending.

response: “I’ve started,” Theo says. “It’s very freeing. You’d hate it.” He lies back on the comforter in the wet jeans and the cashmere, hay and all, and drags one corner of it over himself.
At 6:30 the window is going from gray to white. Jack lies back with the Williams on his chest, meaning to close his eyes for a minute.

“It has to be *encouraged*, Costigan,” Theo says gravely. “It doesn’t have a pump. Nobody tells you that. The heart gets all the press.” He lies down on top of the comforter, sandy feet and all, and falls asleep in the middle of a sentence about lymph nodes.
At 6:30 the window is going from gray to white. Jack lies back with the Williams on his chest, meaning to close his eyes for a minute.

Jack says nothing. Theo works the hay out of his sleeve, straw by straw, and the light comes up another shade on the wall between them. “You walked her home,” Theo says. It isn’t a question, and Jack doesn’t answer it like one.
At 6:30 the window is going from gray to white. Jack lies back with the Williams on his chest, meaning to close his eyes for a minute.

body: He wakes at 11:41 with Bernard Williams open on his chest and the crease of the spine printed in his cheek. Sun all over the room. Across the gap Theo is asleep in his clothes, one arm over his eyes, sand on the sheets. The RAZR, on the floor where it fell, has two.

body.text: Eid Mubarak. Lunch at the center on Mission at noon. The Abrahamic bloc is invited. Margot declined in writing.

body: She let him have the first half. She isn’t giving him the second.

choices.key: You spent Sunday afternoon at Sully’s with Lena and Dale.
